claims.claim: AER citation: 'Growth in a Time of Debt', American Economic Review Papers and Proceedings 100(2), May 2010, pp. 573-78
claims.passage: Title: Growth in a Time of Debt; Journal: American Economic Review; Vol. 100, No. 2; May 2010; Pages: 573-78
claims.notes: AEA page confirms the citation details.

claims.claim: it found that "median growth rates for countries with public debt over roughly 90 percent of GDP are about one percent lower than otherwise; (mean) growth rates are several percent lower."
claims.passage: median growth rates for countries with public debt over roughly 90 percent of GDP are about one percent lower than otherwise; (mean) growth rates are several percent lower" (RR 2010a p. 573).
claims.notes: Verbatim as quoted by HAP.

claims.claim: Its table put average growth above 90% at -0.1%, against 2.8% in the 60% to 90% bucket (also ledger 2.8%, chart published[2]=2.8 labeled 'Reinhart and Rogoff 2010')
claims.passage: RR 2010a Figure 2 (approximated) 4.1    2.9  3.4  -0.1 / RR 2010b Appendix Table 1         4.1   2.8  2.8  -0.1
claims.notes: 2.8 is from the NBER working paper (2010b) Appendix Table 1; the AER paper cited (2010a) is a figure approximated by HAP at 3.4 (and 2.9 for 30-60), so 'its table' and the AER citation misattribute the 60-90 value and the discrepancy is not disclosed.

claims.claim: Covering 20 advanced economies from 1946 to 2009
claims.passage: RR examines three data samples: 20 advanced economies over 1946-2009; the same 20 economies over roughly 200 years; and 20 emerging market economies 1970-2009.
claims.notes: True of the postwar sample; the paper also had a 200-year and an emerging-market sample, which the body mentions only in the fix section.

claims.claim: The authors' website listed 76 high-profile media features.
claims.passage: Reinhart's and Rogoff's website lists 76 high-profile features, including The Economist, Wall Street Journal...
claims.notes: As reported by HAP, site visited 7 April 2013; website not fetched and date not given in the exhibit.

claims.claim: Google Scholar found more than 500 results citing it, excluding the authors' own.
claims.passage: A Google Scholar search for the publication excluding pieces by the authors themselves finds more than 500 results. ... yielded 538 Google Scholar results on 7 April 2013).
claims.notes: Matches; HAP's own search dated 7 April 2013 (date omitted in exhibit).

claims.claim: HAP reported in 2013 that it was the only evidence cited on debt and growth in the 'Paul Ryan Budget'
claims.passage: RR 2010a is the only evidence cited in the "Paul Ryan Budget" on the consequences of high public debt for economic growth.
claims.notes: Reported by HAP and labelled as such; budget document not fetched, disclosed in disclosure.

claims.claim: Path to Prosperity called it 'conclusive empirical evidence' that debt over 90% 'has a significant negative effect on economic growth.'
claims.passage: The study found conclusive empirical evidence that gross debt (meaning all debt that a government owes, including debt held in government trust funds) exceeding 90 percent of the economy has a significant negative eect on economic growth. (Ryan 2013 p. 78)
claims.notes: Quote matches HAP's reproduction ('eect' is a PDF ligature artifact); budget text itself not fetched, but the exhibit says it is as reported by HAP.

claims.claim: HAP recalculated the table. They got 2.2%. (ledger HAP 90%+ 2.2%; verdict 2.2% in the replication)
claims.passage: the average real GDP growth rate for countries carrying a public-debt-to-GDP ratio of over 90 percent is actually 2.2 percent, not -0.1 percent as published in Reinhart and Rogoff.
claims.notes: Confirmed; this is HAP's own calculation from a working spreadsheet supplied by RR, which is not public.

claims.claim: Ledger/chart: HAP corrected 4.2, 3.1, 3.2, 2.2; published 4.1, 2.8, 2.8, -0.1
claims.passage: Country-year weighting, all data  4.2   3.1  3.2  2.2 ... RR 2010b Appendix Table 1         4.1   2.8  2.8  -0.1
claims.notes: Chart DATA matches Table 3 rows; see claim 3 for the AER-vs-NBER caveat on the published series.

claims.claim: a formula averaged lines 30 to 44 instead of 30 to 49, which dropped Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada and Denmark entirely
claims.passage: A coding error in the RR working spreadsheet entirely excludes five countries, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Canada, and Denmark, from the analysis. ... RR averaged cells in lines 30 to 44 instead of lines 30 to 49.
claims.notes: Matches.

claims.claim: "The omitted countries are selected alphabetically."
claims.passage: The omitted countries are selected alphabetically and, hence, likely randomly with respect to economic relationships.
claims.notes: Truncated quote, wording intact.

claims.claim: early years left out for Australia, Canada and New Zealand; NZ excluded years grew 7.7, 11.9, -9.9 and 10.8 percent; what remained was 1 year, 1951, at -7.6%
claims.passage: Real GDP growth rates in those years were 7.7, 11.9, -9.9, and 10.8 percent. After the exclusion of these years, New Zealand contributes only one year to the highest public debt/GDP category, 1951, with a real GDP growth rate of -7.6 percent.
claims.notes: Matches. Erratum item 3 says 1948-49 inclusion was a coding correction per the original summary table, which the exhibit omits.

claims.claim: Britain contributed 19 years averaging 2.4%. New Zealand contributed its 1 year. With 7 countries in the bucket, that year carried 14.3% of the weight. A transcription error then moved it to -7.9%.
claims.passage: real GDP growth in the UK averaged 2.4 percent per year during the 19 years ... the country contributes -7.9 percent growth for a full 14.3 percent (one-seventh) ... leaving seven countries in the highest category in RR.
claims.notes: All inputs trace.

claims.claim: 1 year of New Zealand weighed the same as 19 years of Britain
claims.passage: But equal weighting by country gives a one-year episode as much weight as nearly two decades in the above 90 percent public debt/GDP range.
claims.notes: UK 19 years and NZ 1 year each carry 1/7 weight in the published calculation; this holds only because the 4 NZ years were excluded.

claims.claim: The paper reported 96 country-years above 90%. HAP found 110. The calculation used 71.
claims.passage: RR reports 96 country-years in the highest public debt/GDP category. Our corrected analysis finds 110 country-years ... RR in fact estimated GDP growth in the highest public debt/GDP category with only 71 country-years of data
claims.notes: Matches.

claims.claim: Excluding New Zealand's years and weighting by country together accounted for "a very substantial 1.9 percentage points".
claims.passage: The combined effect of excluding the years for New Zealand and equally weighting the countries (rather than weighting by country-years) reduces the measured average real GDP growth in the highest public debt category by a very substantial 1.9 percentage points.
claims.notes: Table 3 check: 2.2 minus 0.3 (exclusion + weights) = 1.9. Correct combination.

claims.claim: The spreadsheet and transcription errors added 0.4. (verdictNote: together with a transcription slip it moved the result by 0.4 of a point)
claims.passage: The spreadsheet and transcription errors account for an additional -0.4 percentage point.
claims.notes: Table 3: 0.3 (excl + weights) to -0.1 (all four) = 0.4. Correct combination. Note spreadsheet error alone is 0.3 in Table 3 (same as exclusion alone and weights alone), so 'the small one' is order-dependent.

claims.claim: The real gap between the top 2 buckets was 1.0 point; overstated by 2.3, "a factor of nearly two and a half."
claims.passage: The actual gap between the highest and next highest debt/GDP categories is 1.0 percentage point (i.e., 3.2 percent less 2.2 percent). In other words, with their estimate that average GDP growth in the above-90-percent public debt/GDP group is -0.1 percent, RR overstates the gap by 2.3 percentage points or a factor of nearly two and a half.

claims.claim: Most of the distance came from a decision: average each country, then count each country once ... Nobody had to type anything wrong for that to happen.
claims.passage: Country weights only              4.0   3.0  3.0  1.9 ... Selective years exclusion only    4.2   3.1  3.2  1.9
claims.notes: Weighting alone moves the result 0.3 (2.2 to 1.9); the 1.9 is a joint effect of weighting AND the NZ year exclusion, which the erratum says was in part a coding correction (NZ 1948-49 'as stated in the summary table'), so 'nobody typed anything wrong' and 'a decision' overreach.

claims.claim: Title/category: 'The spreadsheet error was the small one'; 'the weighting did the work'
claims.passage: Spreadsheet error only            4.2   3.0  3.2  1.9
claims.notes: Spreadsheet error alone is 0.3, equal to each of the other 2 alone; the 0.4 vs 1.9 split is HAP's ordering of interactive effects, not a standalone ranking.

claims.claim: On 5 May 2013 the authors published an erratum thanking HAP "for pointing out an important correction"
claims.passage: May 5, 2013 ... The authors wish to thank Thomas Herndon, Michael Ash, and Robert Pollin (HAP) for the careful attention and for pointing out an important correction to our original Growth in a Time of Debt.
claims.notes: Date and quote match.

claims.claim: "a coding error that causes the first five countries in the alphabet to be omitted"
claims.passage: (i) a coding error that causes the first five countries in the alphabet to be omitted in forming averages for the 1946-2009 period in one figure
claims.notes: Quote matches; note the erratum is describing HAP's assertion and later confirms the error.

claims.claim: the postwar mean above 90% moves from -0.1% to 0.3%, the median from 1.6% to 1.9%
claims.passage: Post war Mean 4.1 2.8 2.8 -0.1(0.0) ... Median 4.2 3.0 2.9 1.6 ... Coding corrected ... Post war Mean 4.0 3.0 2.5 0.3 ... Median 3.9 3.0 2.9 1.9
claims.notes: Figures trace to the coding-corrected panel; the published cell is -0.1 with (0.0) after blank-cell cleanup.

claims.claim: -0.1% became 0.3% in the authors' own correction; status: 'corrected the coding error ... and disputed the rest'; 'The correction covers the coding error.'
claims.passage: Final including New Zealand (NZ Historical Statistics GDP) ... Post war Mean 4.2 3.0 2.4 2.0 Median 4.2 3.0 2.9 2.5 ... Final including New Zealand (Maddison GDP) ... Post war Mean 4.2 3.0 2.5 1.0 Median 4.2 3.0 2.9 1.9
claims.notes: 0.3 is only the intermediate coding-corrected panel; the erratum's own final panels (after Spain fill and NZ 1948-49 inclusion) give a postwar mean above 90% of 2.0 or 1.0, which the exhibit omits.

claims.claim: The erratum lists the exclusion and the weighting as HAP's assertions, notes HAP is silent on the longer sample back to the 1800s and on emerging markets
claims.passage: The authors assert that there are three problems ... (ii) "selective exclusion" of 1946-1950 for New Zealand, and (iii) "unconventional weighting of summary statistics." Their paper is silent on the results of the longer sample dating back to the 1800s for most of the advanced economies and the exercise on emerging markets
claims.notes: Accurate; 'the authors' in the erratum means HAP. But erratum also made NZ and Spain changes beyond the coding error.

claims.claim: HAP "fails to mention that our median estimates for the postwar sample are very close in magnitude to the averages that they present."
claims.passage: It also fails to mention that our median estimates for the postwar sample are very close in magnitude to the averages that they present.
claims.notes: Quote matches.

claims.claim: the erratum's own table bears it out: 1.9% against 2.2%
claims.passage: Post war ... Median 3.9 3.0 2.9 1.9 (coding corrected); Median 4.2 3.0 2.9 2.5 (final, NZ Historical Statistics)
claims.notes: 1.9 is the coding-corrected median and equals the Maddison final median; the NZ Historical final median is 2.5, so 1.9 vs 2.2 is a selected pair; 'always close' is the exhibit's gloss on 'very close'.

claims.claim: The figure that was not close was the mean, and the mean was the one under 0.
claims.notes: Published postwar mean -0.1 vs median 1.6 above 90%.

claims.claim: Chart caption: 'The first 3 buckets barely move.'
claims.passage: The errors have relatively small effects on measured average real GDP growth in the lower three public debt/GDP categories.
claims.notes: Moves are +0.1, +0.3, +0.4, consistent with HAP's 'relatively small'.

claims.claim: Ledger: Herndon, Ash and Pollin 2013, 60% to 90%: 3.2%
claims.passage: Country-year weighting, all data  4.2   3.1  3.2  2.2
claims.notes: Matches.

claims.claim: Provenance: HAP's 2.2% and replication figures rest on a working spreadsheet supplied by RR that is not public
claims.passage: We were unable to replicate the RR results from the publicly available country spreadsheet data ... Reinhart and Rogoff kindly provided us with the working spreadsheet from the RR analysis.
claims.notes: Figures trace to HAP and RR's erratum partly concedes them, but the exhibit does not state that HAP's inputs were the non-public working spreadsheet.
